title: Arepas
subtitle: Colombian and Venezuelan cornmeal cakes
excerpt: Thick rounds of pre-cooked cornmeal dough, pan-fried until golden with a crisp shell and a soft, tender inside. Split them open and fill with cheese, beans, or avocado. They are versatile, fast, and naturally gluten-free.
sourceNotes: Arepas have been eaten in Colombia and Venezuela for thousands of years. They pre-date European contact and are made from masarepa, a pre-cooked white cornmeal specific to Latin American cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked arepas and reheat in a dry pan.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the dough and shape the arepas ahead. Cook to order.

content.text: Masarepa (pre-cooked white cornmeal) is sold in Latin American shops and online. Do not use standard cornmeal or polenta -- they will not give the right texture. The dough should be smooth, slightly tacky, and hold its shape when pressed.

items.prepNote: use 300g pre-cooked white cornmeal (masarepa or PAN brand)
use 150g white cheese (queso blanco) -- or crumble feta

content.text: Mix the masarepa, salt, and crumbled cheese in a bowl. Add the warm water or milk gradually, mixing with your hands.
Knead until the dough is smooth and holds together. It should not crack when shaped. Add a little more water if it does.
Rest for 5 minutes. Divide into 8 equal balls.
Press each ball between your palms into a round disc about 1.5cm thick.
Heat oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Cook the arepas for 5 to 6 minutes per side until golden and crisp.
Rest for 2 minutes. Split open with a knife and fill as you like.

items.cause: Too little water or not rested long enough
items.fix: Add water a tablespoon at a time and knead until the dough no longer cracks. Rest for at least 5 minutes.

items.symptom: Arepas are golden outside but raw inside
items.fix: Lower the heat to medium-low. Arepas need longer on a moderate heat to cook through without burning.
Keep them at least 1.5cm thick. They do not rise during cooking so what you shape is what you get.

content.text: Arepas are one of the oldest foods in South America. They pre-date European colonisation by thousands of years and are eaten daily in Colombia and Venezuela as breakfast, snack, or side. In Venezuela, arepas are filled and eaten as a main meal. In Colombia, they tend to be thinner and served alongside other dishes. Both countries regard the arepa as a national symbol.
